attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post; not quoting anyone else.

semantics.note: The firm part is the present-tense remark about obvious truthiness problems. 'Jury is still out' only expresses uncertainty and is correctly left unscored.

contract.note: Plain reading is fair. It scores whether chat-style search showed public factual errors up to the post date. The Feb 1–12 window and including Bard are ordinary readings of 'current'.

evidence.note: The Verge, Feb 8, 2023, reports Bard's demo answer wrongly crediting JWST with the first exoplanet image, with astronomers' corrections.
Reuters, Feb 8, 2023, independently confirms the same Bard error and Google's statement that testing is needed. Both predate the post.
Google's own Feb 6 announcement presents Bard as experimental and web-informed. This sets the product scope but says nothing about errors.

reviews.rationale: Two independent reports, both dated before the Feb 12 post, document a verifiable factual error in Bard's launch demo. That meets the support condition for obvious current truthiness problems. No evidence shows the error was misreported. The 'how far it can get' part is uncertainty and is not scored.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his post, about LLMs and content farms.

semantics.note: In context, the sentence says LLMs make content-farm text cheap and therefore more widespread. Calling it a causal mechanism with no deadline is faithful.

contract.note: Plain reading, lower cost leading to more output or more sites, is an ordinary and fair one. Requiring evidence that links cost savings to more output is a reasonable test of the causal claim.

evidence.note: NewsGuard (May 2023) found 49 mostly AI-written content-farm sites, some publishing hundreds of articles a day. This partly supports the claim about volume but gives no cost or pre-LLM baseline.
About 25 newly identified sites a week. But newly detected is not the same as newly created, and the report doesn't measure costs, so this can't show the causal link.
A 2025 survey of marketers finds AI content about 4.7x cheaper. The population is marketers, not content farms, and the survey doesn't link savings to output.

reviews.rationale: The evidence shows AI-written content farms producing at high volume and that AI content is cheaper in a different population. No item connects lower costs to more content-farm output or new sites, as the contract requires, and the packet's own stated gaps say so. Nothing contradicts the claim. The causal claim stays unresolved.
